Title: Tunable Nonlinear Activation Functions Enabled by WO₃ Films for Adaptive Diffractive Deep Neural Networks
Text:

Tunable Nonlinear Activation Functions Enabled by WO3
Films for Adaptive Diﬀractive Deep Neural Networks
Xiaoguang Ma, Fangzhen Hu, Xi Chen, Zhecheng Qiu, Min Gu,* and Qiming Zhang*
Conventional electronics face intrinsic bandwidth and power constraints in
deep learning, fueling the pursuit of optical computing’s parallel processing
and energy eﬃciency. A critical roadblock for optical neural networks (ONNs)
lies in the missing trainable-tunable nonlinear activation mechanisms
required for modeling complex data correlations and cross-task
generalization. Here, this limitation is overcome through engineered tungsten
trioxide (WO3) thin ﬁlms with dynamically controllable nonlinearity. Z-scan
measurements demonstrate stoichiometry-dependent nonlinear responses
modulated via photogenerated coloration, enabling precise control of optical
nonlinearities. The ﬁlms’ non-volatile memory eﬀects permit implementation
of adaptive in-memory computing architectures where activation functions
are trainable and task-speciﬁcally optimized. This reconﬁgurable nonlinearity
framework enhances both learning capability and generalization performance
in ONNs, while achieving high-performance THz-scale response speeds (1
THz) for real-time adaptive computing. Integrated as programmable
activation layers in optical diﬀraction networks, the system demonstrates
classiﬁcation accuracy improvements of 4.62% (MNIST), 3.29%
(Fashion-MNIST), 13.53% (KMNIST), and 12.2% (CIFAR-10). The synergistic
combination of non-volatile tunability, ultrafast reconﬁguration, and
stoichiometric control positions WO3 thin ﬁlms as a disruptive materials
platform, resolving long-standing activation function limitations in photonic
neuromorphic systems while enabling adaptive high-performance optical
processors through on-demand nonlinear engineering.
1. Introduction
The rapid advancement of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has had a
profound impact on global economic recovery, social progress,
and human lives.[1,2] Conventional computers, however, face sub-
stantial challenges related to energy consumption,[3] computing

separation of storage and computation
inherent in the Von Neumann architec-
ture. Moreover, the limitations of Moore’s
Law have compelled researchers to seek
alternative solutions.[6] In contrast, op-
tical neural networks (ONNs) integrate
optical technologies with artiﬁcial intel-
ligence, harnessing the speed and par-
allelism of light to outperform tradi-
tional electronic systems. As a result,
ONNs have emerged as a promising
paradigm for fast and energy-eﬃcient
computation.[7–9] The key advantage of
ONNs lies in their ability to process vast
amounts of data simultaneously, mak-
ing them particularly suitable for tasks
such as image classiﬁcation, natural lan-
guage processing, and complex decision-
making.[10–14] Recent advancements have
demonstrated the potential of ONNs to
deliver enhanced speed and energy ef-
ﬁciency. However, intrinsic limitations,
especially those related to linear func-
tions, persist. Although eﬀective in clas-
sical neural networks, these linear func-
tions limit ONNs’ ability to capture the
intricate nonlinear relationships inher-
ent in real-world data.
Nonlinear
activation
functions
are
widely recognized for enhancing the
representational capacity of neural networks. Nonlinearity en-
ables networks to learn complex patterns, thereby improv-
ing generalization and performance across various tasks.[15–17]
In electronic neural networks, nonlinear activation functions
such as ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh have eﬀectively improved
performance. However, achieving comparable nonlinear re-
sponses in optical materials remains a signiﬁcant challenge,
restricting their optical counterparts.[18–20] Incorporating non-
linear optical elements into ONNs presents signiﬁcant chal-
lenges, creating a gap in addressing complex tasks and ne-
cessitating innovative designs for eﬀective nonlinear activation
layers.
Recent research has explored various methods for integrat-
ing nonlinearities into optical systems. Nonlinear activation re-
sponses in photonic neurons can be realized through all-optical
or optoelectronic nonlinearities. Electro-optical conversion[20–22]
limits the multilayer cascading in optical networks, signiﬁ-
cantly constraining the scalability and energy eﬃciency of op-

tical computation.[23–25] Thus, an all-optical approach is essen-
tial for the large-scale deployment and high-speed application of
neural networks. All-optical neural networks (AONNs) can uti-
lize materials such as phase-change materials (PCMs),[26] sat-
urable absorption (SA) in thermal atoms,[27] ferroelectric thin
ﬁlms,[28,29] laser-cooled 85Rb atoms with electromagnetically
induced transparency,[30] and 2D metal carbides and nitrides
(MXene).[15,16]
The development of AONNs is impeded by the limited
nonlinear optical response of conventional materials, restrict-
ing their utility as photonic neurons.[16,31–33] While engineered
nonlinear materials and nanostructures oﬀer enhanced perfor-
mance, their slow recovery times (on the nanosecond scale)
and dependence on external energy inputs hinder high-speed
optical computation. Furthermore, existing platforms demon-
strate poor generalization across multi-task learning and com-
plex real-world scenarios. Addressing these challenges requires
a material platform with trainable nonlinearities, real-time
adaptability, and scalable 3D integration for energy-eﬃcient
ONNs.
Tungsten trioxide (WO3) stands as a superior candidate for
all-optical nonlinear activators due to its defect-engineered gi-
ant optical nonlinearity, picosecond photonic response, and di-
rect photon-driven operation, eliminating electro-optic conver-
sion losses. Critically, electrochemical modulation of oxygen
vacancies enables a giant nonlinear absorption coeﬃcient up
to 632 cm GW−1—providing reconﬁgurable saturable-to-reverse
saturable absorption thresholds for activation functions.[34,35] The
picosecond response speed, essential for neuromorphic comput-
ing, is demonstrated by transient absorption techniques, reveal-
ing rapid fs-to-ps carrier dynamics.[36] Moreover, optically con-
trolled nonlinearities do not require electro-optical conversion
and directly utilize photon-material interactions to reduce delay
and energy loss.[37] These synergistic properties position WO3 as
a transformative platform for high-speed, energy-eﬃcient pho-
tonic neural networks.
In this study, we introduce a novel approach that exploits
the unique properties of WO3 ﬁlms to dynamically regulate
nonlinear optical responses in diﬀractive deep neural net-
works (DDNNs). Unlike conventional materials, WO3 com-
bines nonvolatile phase-change behavior with optically tunable
nonlinearity, facilitating stable nonlinear activation states with-
out the need for continuous energy input. Using Z-scan tech-
niques and pump-probe transient absorption measurements,
we demonstrate the dynamic modulation of WO3 ﬁlms’ non-
linear properties, further elucidating the distinct nonlinear re-
sponses of WO3-1 and WO3-2 ﬁlms. Furthermore, we performed
benchmark machine learning tasks using an optical diﬀrac-
tion model in the free-space domain. By incorporating opti-
cally measured tunable activation functions, we achieved sig-
niﬁcant improvements in accuracy across diverse datasets, in-
cluding MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, KMNIST, and CIFAR-10. The
adaptive nonlinear response of WO3 ﬁlms allows real-time re-
conﬁguration of computational behavior, overcoming gener-
alization limitations in multi-task scenarios. These attributes
position WO3 as a transformative candidate for high-speed
optical computing, artiﬁcial intelligence, and data-intensive
applications.
2. Results and Discussion
Figure 1 depicts an all-optical DDNN architecture integrated with
a WO3-based nonlinear activation layer. The nonlinear properties
of the WO3 ﬁlm were systematically quantiﬁed via a custom non-
linear optical setup, with its response characterized after variable
durations of UV irradiation, as shown in Figure 1a.
Figure 1b illustrates a generic deep neural network architec-
ture comprising an input layer, an output layer, and hidden lay-
ers. This feedforward structure consists of interconnected neu-
rons operating without closed loops, each neuron connecting ex-
clusively to successive layers. Each neuron performs two core op-
tical functions: a linear operation unit executing weighted sum-
mation and a nonlinear unit transforming inputs into neuron
outputs. In this work, the nonlinear unit is implemented using a
WO3 nanoribbon ﬁlm, with its experimentally measured nonlin-
ear response ﬁtted and shown in the inset.
The implemented DDNN consists of an input layer, diﬀractive
layers, a WO3 nonlinear layer, and an output layer (Figure 1c).
DDNNs leverage light diﬀraction to perform computational tasks
analogous to conventional neural networks. Input optical ﬁelds
(e.g., encoded images) interact with engineered diﬀractive layers
that modulate both phase and amplitude. Sequentially arranged
diﬀractive layers process light propagation, emulating neuron-
like operations including weighted summation. Critically, the
WO3 nonlinear layer enables dynamic nonlinearity tuning via UV
excitation, which modiﬁes the complex amplitude distribution
post-diﬀraction. The resulting output ﬁeld is detected and de-
coded to yield computational results, such as classiﬁcation or pre-
diction.
Photochromic materials have become a major focus in mod-
ern materials science and optical engineering. Their ability to
reversibly alter optical properties under light irradiation renders
them promising candidates for various applications.[33] Defects,
including localized defects, impurities, and dislocations, play cru-
cial roles in WO3 photochromism. Intervalent electron transfer
between tungsten ions with diﬀering valence states is considered
a key factor facilitating photochromism. Upon light irradiation,
the WO3 ﬁlm generates electrons (e−) and holes (h+). Electrons
enter the conduction band of WO3, while holes react with ad-
sorbed surface water to form H+ ions, which subsequently dif-
fuse into WO3.[38] This series of reactions ultimately induces a
color change (Figure S1, Supporting Information). This mecha-
nism provides the foundation for further exploration and appli-
cation of WO3’s photochromic properties.
The WO3 ﬁlms were directly grown on FTO substrates us-
ing a simple hydrothermal method, without the need for a seed
layer (Figure 2a). Detailed preparation methods are provided in
the Experimental Section. In situ Raman experiments conﬁrmed
that H+ intercalation occurred during the UV light-induced col-
oration of WO3.[38] As illustrated in Figure 2b,c, the Raman
spectra of WO3 ﬁlms at diﬀerent UV irradiation times (aver-
age power: 1.696 mW) and their corresponding recovery pro-
cesses are presented. The pristine ﬁlms do not display strong
resonance peaks. However, with increasing UV irradiation time,
the ﬁlms gradually show prominent resonance peaks at 794, 696,
and 249 cm−1. The bands at 696 and 794 cm−1 correspond to
the O─W─O stretching vibrations of the bridging oxygen atoms,

As the UV irradiation time increases from 5 to 9 min, the
Raman signal intensity gradually increases. Moreover, the res-
onance peak at 794 cm−1 shifts to 796 cm−1, while the peaks
at 696 and 249 cm−1 shift to 693 and 246 cm−1, respectively.
The strongest peak, shifting from 803 to 811 cm−1, can be at-
tributed to the shortening of the W─O bond due to the increased
negative charge between tungsten atoms.[39,40] During the recov-
ery process, the Raman signal intensity gradually diminishes,
and a new peak emerges at 945 cm−1. The displacement of the
Raman peaks with increasing irradiation time indicates struc-
tural changes in the samples during UV exposure. After suﬃ-
cient recovery from bleaching, the Raman peaks return to their
original positions, conﬁrming that the structural changes are
reversible during the transition between photochromism and
bleaching.
To determine their linear optical properties, the absorption
spectra of the WO3-1 and WO3-2 ﬁlms are shown in Figure 2d,e,
respectively. The optical absorption intensity increases signiﬁ-
cantly as the wavelength decreases from the near-infrared (NIR)
to the UV range. From the inset Tauc plot calculations in
Figure 2d,e, WO3 is identiﬁed as an indirect bandgap semicon-
ductor with bandgap values of ≈2.18 eV for WO3-1 and 3.05 eV
for WO3-2. The detailed fabrication process of the WO3 ﬁlms is
provided in the Experimental Section. The side view of the WO3
nanoribbon ﬁlms, shown in Figure 2f,g, reveals thicknesses of
≈1.675 and 1.920 μm for WO3-1 and WO3-2, respectively.
Photographs of WO3 ﬁlms after diﬀerent durations of UV ir-
radiation are shown in Figure S2 (Supporting Information). Fur-
thermore, scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)
and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping results
(Figure 2h,i) conﬁrm the successful synthesis of WO3 nanorib-
bons. The mapping reveals the spatial distribution of four typical
elements: W (purple), O (green), Sn (cyan), and C (red), which
overlap well, further validating the successful synthesis of WO3
nanoribbons. Additionally, Figure S3 (Supporting Information)
presents SEM images of WO3-1 and WO3-2 nanoribbon ﬁlms
captured at diﬀerent magniﬁcations.
The nonlinear optical (NLO) response of WO3 can be dynam-
ically modulated through external optical excitation. The modu-
lation characteristics are strongly dependent on the duration of
UV lamp irradiation. Prior to conducting Z-scan measurements
of the open apertures, the WO3 ﬁlm was irradiated with a 275 nm
UV lamp for varying durations, and probing was performed at a
near-infrared wavelength of 800 nm. Nonlinear response mea-
surements of the optically controlled WO3 ﬁlm were carried out
using the optical setup shown in Figure 3a.
Dynamic modulation of the nonlinear activation function,
based on the nonlinear response of phase-change materials
(PCMs), is essential for enhancing the computational and rea-
soning capabilities of optical neural networks. Using the Z-scan
method, we investigated the nonlinear properties of the WO3
ﬁlm throughout the entire process of photochromism and re-
covery from UV lamp irradiation. As shown in Figure 3b,e,h,
a transmission-type aperture test was conducted on the WO3-1
ﬁlms. Under UV lamp irradiation, the transmittance increases,
exhibiting a typical saturated absorption (SA) phenomenon,
as electrons are fermions and must obey the Pauli-blocking
principle. The photon energy of the excitation signiﬁcantly ex-
ceeds the 2.18 eV bandgap. When the laser excites the sam-
ple, electrons undergo interband transitions by absorbing pho-
tons. Due to the band-ﬁlling eﬀect, the transition probability
decreases with increasing laser intensity, resulting in higher
transmittance.

and incident light intensity (I), as described by a two-level model.

Furthermore, after 10 s and 9 min of UV lamp irradiation,
we examined the nonlinear refraction of the original and UV-
irradiated WO3-1 ﬁlms using 120 fs femtosecond pulses at a
wavelength of 800 nm. The WO3-1 ﬁlms consistently exhibited
self-focusing properties, with distinct valleys observed during the
coloring stage, corresponding to a positive nonlinear refractive

tial ﬁlm, as shown in Figure 3d,g,j. Similarly, we conducted both

process of WO3-1 ﬁlms. The results show that nonlinear absorp-

index presents a valley-peak conﬁguration (Figure S4, Support-
ing Information). The saturation intensity during the process ini-
tially increases and subsequently decreases. After 16.5 h of re-
covery, the saturation intensity of the WO3-1 ﬁlm returns to a
value close to its initial state, further conﬁrming the material’s
reversibility.
Subsequently, we conducted Z-scan measurements on the
WO3-2 ﬁlms with both open- and closed-aperture setups. Notably,
the WO3-2 ﬁlms exhibited a nonlinear response that diﬀered sig-
niﬁcantly from that of the WO3-1 ﬁlms. As the UV lamp irradi-

to 9 min, reverse saturation absorption (RSA) was detected. Con-
currently, the nonlinear refractive index exhibited a peak-valley
proﬁle, indicative of self-defocusing properties (see Figure S5,
Supporting Information). For the RSA response coexistence, we
could get:

The observed diﬀerences between the two WO3 ﬁlms are pri-
marily attributed to variations in their defect characteristics and
optical bandgaps, which inﬂuence their optical and electronic
properties. Speciﬁcally, the defect density, modulated by vari-
ations in oxalic acid concentration during fabrication, plays a
critical role in determining carrier mobility and introducing lo-
calized states that alter the ﬁlms’ optical absorption behavior.
Additionally, the distinct nonlinear absorption behaviors in hy-
drothermally synthesized WO3-1 (bandgap 2.18 eV, Fig. 2d) and
WO3-2 (bandgap 3.05 eV, Fig. 2e) under 800 nm femtosecond
irradiation—manifesting as SA in WO3-1 versus two-photon ab-
sorption (TPA) in WO3-2—primarily arise from bandgap engi-
neering and defect-mediated carrier dynamics.[35] WO3-1 exhibits
bandgap narrowing due to oxygen vacancies, generating mid-gap
defect states ≈0.5–1.0 eV above the valence band. These states fa-
cilitate valence-to-defect transitions, enabling carrier ﬁlling satu-
ration during 275 nm UV pre-irradiation. Consequently, subse-
quent 800 nm excitation (1.55 eV photons) is inhibited by Pauli
blocking, resulting in SA.[35]
Conversely, WO3-2′s wider bandgap and lower defect concen-
tration minimize mid-gap states, precluding signiﬁcant single-
photon absorption at 800 nm. The simultaneous absorption of
two photons (total energy 3.10 eV >bandgap) via a virtual inter-
mediate state enables TPA dominance in the absence of defect-
mediated saturation.[34] This defect engineering approach pro-
vides critical control over WO3’s nonlinear optical responses,
with signiﬁcant implications for photonic devices requiring
switchable SA/TPA functionalities.[36,44–46]
To evaluate the stability of the nonlinear properties of the WO3-
1 ﬁlm, Z-scan data at various intensities are shown in Figure
S7a,c (Supporting Information). After curve ﬁtting, the n2 and
𝛽values, along with the corresponding FOM, were measured as
a function of power before and after two months (Figure S7b,d,
Supporting Information). A comparison of the nonlinearities of
WO3 ﬁlms before and after two months shows that the n2 and𝛽
remain stable, conﬁrming the excellent stability of the ﬁlms.

The relaxation processes of the WO3-1 ﬁlm, pumped with TAS
at 320 nm and probed at 350, 532, and 800 nm, occur within
the picosecond range of 𝜏1 (1–26.5 ps), consistent with previous
reports.[34–36,44] This fast carrier relaxation process governs the re-
covery rate of the nonlinear activator to its original state within,
which is crucial for its dynamic response. As a result, the acti-
vation response of this AONAF (all-optical nonlinear activation
function) reaches up to 1 THz at 320 nm, enabling ultrafast in-
formation processing.
The longer lifetime component 𝜏2 of 13.3 ns in the WO3-1 ﬁlm
indicates extended exciton lifetimes, attributed to higher crys-
tallinity and lower defect density. These properties facilitate ef-
ﬁcient exciton diﬀusion and reduce non-radiative recombination
pathways. The absence of a shift in the PB peak position con-
ﬁrms that bandgap narrowing (BGN), typically caused by strong
carrier-carrier interactions, can be excluded from the analysis.
Additionally, the WO3-2 ﬁlm exhibits greater photoinduced ab-
sorption at 800 nm compared to the WO3-1 ﬁlm. The rapid decay
within less than 10 ps is attributed to direct electron–hole recom-
bination, while the trapping process occurs on a timescale of sev-
eral tens of picoseconds. The long-lived bleaching component is
associated with the recombination of electrons trapped in oxygen
vacancy states.[45,46]
To verify the eﬀect of the dynamic nonlinear activation func-
tion of our WO3 ﬁlms on the performance of optical neural net-
works in the free-space domain, we incorporated the WO3-based
nonlinear activation function into an optical diﬀraction neu-
ral network model to enhance classiﬁcation performance across
multiple benchmark datasets. The PyTorch framework was used
for image recognition and classiﬁcation, utilizing the experimen-
tally measured SA nonlinear activation function across these
datasets. The DDNN simulations were conducted utilizing the
angular spectrum method, with model training implemented
through a combination of cross-entropy and mean-squared er-
ror loss functions. The optimization process employed the Adam
optimizer over 10 training epochs, systematically applied to
three benchmark datasets: MNIST (Modiﬁed National Institute
of Standards and Technology database), Fashion-MNIST (FM-
NIST), and Kuzushiji-MNIST (KMNIST). The results demon-
strated that incorporating these nonlinear activation functions
signiﬁcantly improved classiﬁcation accuracy, emphasizing the
potential of nonlinear optical properties in advancing optical neu-
ral networks.
Figure 5 provides a comprehensive evaluation of the classiﬁ-
cation performance of DDNNs across the MNIST, FMNIST, and
KMNIST datasets. Figure 5a,c,e compares the performance of
DDNNs incorporating tunable nonlinear activation functions de-
rived from SA measurements with those that lack these func-
tions. Incorporating nonlinear activation functions signiﬁcantly
enhanced classiﬁcation accuracy, with improvements of 4.62%,
3.29%, and 13.53% on the MNIST, FMNIST, and KMNIST
datasets, respectively. This improvement is attributed to the dy-
namic response of the nonlinear activation function to varying
input intensities, which eﬀectively captures complex data rela-
tionships and enhances the network’s ability to discern subtle
patterns.
The confusion matrices in Figure 5b,d,f further illustrate the
enhanced classiﬁcation performance. These matrices demon-
strate a marked reduction in misclassiﬁcations when tunable and
trainable nonlinear activation functions are applied, underscor-
ing their critical role in improving the robustness and accuracy
of the DDNNs. Figure 5g,h present the training and testing ac-
curacies achieved by the DDNNs with the measured nonlinear
activation functions across all three datasets. These results un-
derscore the stability and reliability of the activation functions
during both training and inference. Similarly, Figure 5i,j display
the corresponding training and testing contrasts, reinforcing the
consistent performance improvements brought about by the tun-
able nonlinear activation functions.

As shown in Table 1, the proposed trainable and tunable
nonlinear activation function is compared with previously re-
ported methods in terms of nonlinear mechanisms and per-
formance. The results show that the proposed activation func-
tion outperforms existing approaches across multiple datasets,
highlighting its signiﬁcant ability to enhance robustness, adapt-
ability, and classiﬁcation accuracy in optical neural networks.
However, the performance gap between our diﬀractive optical
neural network (DONN, 45.9% accuracy) and electronic bench-
marks (e.g., ResNet-18′s 94.6%) in Table 1 arises from fun-
damental physical-architectural constraints. Bridging the accu-
racy diﬀerential with electronic neural networks necessitates co-
optimized architectural and fabrication innovations. First, optical
skip-connections implemented via beam-splitting elements facil-
itate ResNet/U-Net-inspired feature fusion, enabling dynamic re-
ceptive ﬁeld adaptation for capturing multiscale textures and ﬁne
edge characteristics. Second, extending the number of diﬀrac-
tion layers through advanced 3D integration techniques greatly
expands parameter capacity while preserving sub-picosecond la-
tency. Crucially, enhanced silicon photonics foundry processes
or two-photon nanolithography enable seamless integration of
tunable nonlinear activation functions between diﬀractive lay-
ers. This co-design paradigm leverages established semiconduc-
tor manufacturing while maintaining inherent light-speed ad-
vantages, systematically addressing current limitations in feature
abstraction depth, spatial adaptability, and nonlinear transforma-
tion capabilities—thereby narrowing performance diﬀerences in
complex visual tasks.
To comprehensively assess the adaptability of adjustable non-
linear weights to diverse tasks in DDNNs, we analyzed the con-
vergence trends of two-layer nonlinear weight parameters within
an optical diﬀraction model across four datasets (see Figure S14,
Supporting Information). The results show that for simpler tasks,
such as MNIST, FMNIST, and KMNIST, the nonlinear weights
converge rapidly, with the second-layer weights achieving con-
vergence faster than those of the ﬁrst layer. In contrast, for
more complex tasks, such as CIFAR-10, the convergence pro-
cess is slower. Notably, the ﬁrst-layer weights converge faster
than the second-layer weights, and their magnitudes are consis-
tently smaller. These ﬁndings highlight the ability of the nonlin-
ear weight parameters to adapt dynamically to task complexity,
ensuring optimal performance under varying computational de-
mands.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we have demonstrated the use of WO3 thin ﬁlms as
nonlinear optical activators in ONNs, representing a signiﬁcant
advancement in optical computing. The WO3 ﬁlms exhibit tun-
able nonlinear optical properties, which can be dynamically mod-
ulated through photogenerated coloration processes. This ability
to control the nonlinear response in real time enables the cre-
ation of adaptive activation functions that can be ﬁne-tuned dur-
ing the training process. Importantly, the non-volatile nature of

4. Experimental Section
WO3-1 Film Preparation:
WO3 ﬁlms were synthesized using a
standard hydrothermal method. The precursor solution was pre-
pared by dissolving 0.3042 g of ammonium paratungstate hydrate
(H4nN1nO41W12·xH2O, molecular weight 3042) and 6.3 g of oxalic acid
dihydrate (C2H2O4·2H2O) in 40 g of ethanol. The mixture was sonicated
for 15 min and then transferred to a 50 mL Teﬂon-lined stainless steel au-
toclave. A piece of ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass was placed against
the wall of the autoclave, with the conductive side facing downward. The
autoclave was sealed and kept at 180 °C for 4 h. After the reaction, the
system was cooled to room temperature under ambient conditions. The
resulting ﬁlms were washed with ethanol and air-dried to yield WO3 thin
ﬁlms.
WO3-2 Film Preparation:
The preparation of the WO3-2 ﬁlm followed
the same procedure as described above, except that 12.6 g of oxalic acid
dihydrate (C2H2O4·2H2O) was used. The precursor solution and the sub-
sequent steps remain identical to those outlined previously.
Z-Scan Measurement:
The custom-built Z-scan system used to mea-
sure the nonlinear optical coeﬃcients of the WO3 ﬁlm is shown in
Figure 3a. A femtosecond laser (Spectra-Physics, Solstice Ace) with a cen-
tral wavelength of 800 nm, a pulse repetition rate of 5 kHz, and a pulse
duration of 120 fs was used for Z-scan characterization. The collimated
800 nm femtosecond laser beam, directed through a pair of reﬂective mir-
rors and an optical chopper, was used as the reference light. Notably, the
800 nm wavelength used here functions solely as the detection light, with-
out inducing further photoactivation of the WO3 ﬁlm. A half-wave plate
(Thorlabs, AHWP10M-980) and a Glan laser prism (Thorlabs, GL10-B)
were used to precisely control the laser beam’s polarization and intensity.
To prevent damage to the photomultiplier tube (Thorlabs, PMM02), an
adjustable neutral density ﬁlter (Hengyang Optics, GT-060101) was posi-
tioned in front of the detector. The WO3 ﬁlm sample was placed on a mo-
torized stage (Newport, DL325) for precise positional adjustments. A f =
150 mm biconvex lens (Newport, KBX070) focused the femtosecond laser
beam through the 4f system onto the sample. Optical power was moni-
tored using a Multibase photomultiplier tube (Thorlabs, PMM02). Due to
the weak detected signal, the signal-to-noise ratio was improved using an
optical chopper (Thorlabs, MC2000B) in combination with a lock-in am-
pliﬁer (Zurich Instruments, MFLI). Motorized stage movement and data
acquisition were synchronized using a LabVIEW program.
Characterization:
Raman spectroscopy was performed using a high-
resolution research-grade spectrometer (Andor Shamrock 500i) with a
532 nm excitation laser. UV–vis absorption spectra of the ﬁlms were ac-
quired using a Shimadzu 3600 UV–vis spectrophotometer. The surface
morphology and elemental composition of the ﬁlms were analyzed using
a ZEISS Sigma 300 ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscope (SEM)
equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) module, op-
erated at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV.
Adaptive DDNN Simulation:
All-optical simulations of adaptive
DDNNs were performed using four benchmark datasets: MNIST, Fashion-
MNIST, KMNIST, and CIFAR-10. The MNIST handwritten digit dataset
originally contained 60 000 training and 10 000 testing grayscale images
(28 × 28 pixels) distributed across 10 numerical categories (0–9). Follow-
ing the same structural paradigm, Fashion-MNIST comprised 70 000 gar-
ment images representing 10 fashion classes, while KMNIST incorporated
70 000 historical Japanese cursive characters from 10 classical categories.
The CIFAR-10 dataset provided 60 000 natural images (32 × 32 pixels)
across 10 object classes, with RGB channels converted to single-channel
grayscale via luminance-weighted averaging to ensure optical system com-
patibility. Standardized subsets of 6000 training and 1000 testing images
were randomly extracted from each dataset for systematic benchmark-
ing. The DDNN architecture employed a training protocol combining for-
ward propagation-based loss calculation with stochastic gradient descent
(SGD) backpropagation for weight optimization, utilizing an SGD opti-
mizer featuring cosine-decay learning rate (lr) scheduling (initial lr = 0.01)
and mini-batch processing (batch size = 10). Models for MNIST, Fashion-
MNIST, and KMNIST completed 10 training epochs, whereas CIFAR-10 re-
quired an extended 50-epoch training to address heightened feature com-
plexity. The adaptive DDNN framework implemented angular spectrum
method-based propagation modeling, enhanced by a hybrid loss function
combining cross-entropy classiﬁcation error with mean-squared output
regularization. Nonlinear optical operations were incorporated through
material-speciﬁc transfer functions derived from experimental WO3 pho-
tochromic characteristics, where the dynamic transmittance-power rela-
tionship during photochromism was integrated into the optical diﬀrac-
tion model to emulate nonlinear activation mechanisms. This approach
enabled quantitative estimation of tunable nonlinearities’ impact on net-
work functionality, with complete implementation details provided in the
Supporting Information.
